newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian PM waits to see if crisis resolved.
newsitem.headline: Albanian PM waits to see if crisis resolved.

text.p: Plans for Albania's elections hung in the balance on Thursday after Prime Minister Bashkim Fino appealed for intensive international monitoring and political parties dithered over whether to take part in the vote.

Albania, still crackling with tension after the riots and looting of March, has appealed for full "Bosnia-style" monitoring of elections planned for June 29 as a way of persuading political parties to take part in the vote.
"The government has done its job and waits for a positive reply from special envoy Vranitzky," Fino's spokesman said.
The government made its appeal for international help on Wednesday to persuade political parties to drop threats to boycott the vote over election rules they say favour President Sali Berisha.
Franz Vranitzky, special envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), was to make a report in Vienna on the political crisis in the anarchic Balkan state.

One politician said Albania needed the same kind of all-embracing monitoring of its election as in Bosnia. Last year's voting there was largely organised by outside bodies such as the OSCE, which mobilised a large force to help compile voter registers and monitor every polling station.
The request was made after political parties refused to stand in the vote, accusing Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party of passing election laws that were aimed at making them the winners.

The Socialist Party, the second-largest party and main rival to the Democrats, has said it will stand even with the current law if the international community guarantees that the elections will be free and fair.
A spokesman for the Socialists said the party leadership was meeting behind closed doors finally to decide whether to take part in the election or not.
Other parties were not immediately available to say whether they were considering taking part.
The Socialists pulled out of the last poll in May 1996, accusing the Democrats of rigging the vote. That election was called seriously flawed by the OSCE.
"We will take part in the elections only if full guarantees are given by international institutions," Socialist chairman Fatos Nano told newspaper Gazeta Shqiptare.

The elections are seen as vital to restore order to Albania, which was engulfed by an uprising in March after people took to the streets in fury at losing all their money in collapsed pyramid investment schemes.
The country is far calmer but violence continues throughout the former Stalinist state, with killings and shootings taking place almost daily.
Swathes of the country remain outside government control, particularly the south, which blamed Berisha for the collapse of the schemes and saw the worst violence.
The international community has sent a barrage of warnings to Albania, saying aid and assistance which the impoverished country vitally needs may be withdrawn if they do not go ahead.
Italy, leader of a 6,000-strong multinational force that is protecting the aid supplies, has said the troops may pull out if the elections do not take place.
